title: What is speech therapy?
intro: Speech and language therapy helps people with difficulties in speaking, understanding, reading, voice, fluency or swallowing. It is provided by trained therapists to children and adults, and aims to improve communication and quality of life.

sections.heading: Who it helps
paragraphs: Children with delayed speech, unclear pronunciation, stuttering or language disorders, and adults who have lost speech after stroke or brain injury, with voice problems, Parkinson's disease, or difficulty swallowing. People after laryngeal surgery and those with hearing loss also benefit.

sections.heading: What therapists do
paragraphs: They assess speech, language, voice and swallowing with tests and observation. They then plan therapy with exercises and strategies, for example practising sounds, building vocabulary, improving fluency, training the voice or teaching safe swallowing. They also train family and teachers and may recommend communication aids.

sections.heading: What sessions involve
paragraphs: Sessions are usually weekly, individual or in groups, often using games for children. Practice at home is important. The length of therapy depends on the problem, from a few weeks to years. Progress is reviewed regularly and goals adjusted.

sections.heading: Getting speech therapy
paragraphs: A doctor typically prescribes it, and health insurance may cover it, depending on country and rules. Waiting times can be long, so ask early. Early help is most effective in children, but adults also gain from therapy even years after an injury.

sections.heading: What families can do
paragraphs: Talk, read and play with children, give them time to respond, avoid correcting too much and praise efforts. For adults with speech problems, be patient, reduce noise, use simple sentences and give extra time. Join support groups if helpful.

examples.title: Practising at home
examples.text: Imagine your child has therapy for unclear sounds. You could play the sound games daily for a few minutes.

examples.title: Supporting communication
examples.text: Suppose a parent has lost speech after a stroke. You might speak slowly, ask yes-or-no questions and give time to answer.
